messages.subject: Translation of examples in Hill, Gelman books into Stan code
parts:
Hi,

I am new to this group, so forgive me if this is the incorrect place to post this. I wanted to help by translating some existing examples in the aforementioned books (and maybe some others, for example some in Lee's book on 'Bayesian cognitive modelling') into working Stan code. I am newish to Stan; having used BUGS previously, but have been using it to successfully fit some hierarchical models that I previously struggled with, over the last couple of months. It may take me a bit longer than more experienced Stan developers to code some examples, but am hopeful I can contribute!

I am aware that there is already considerable effort to 'translate'/make working Stan code for the books I mentioned, and so wanted to ask - has work begun on writing Stan code for Gelman, Hill and other books? I can see that the majority of BUGS book examples are done already. Also, where would be most helpful for me to begin?

Best,

Ben Lambert

What we want is someone to take a pass over all the
models and make sure they're up to our current thinking
in terms of priors, coding efficiency, and coding style.

We'd ideally like to have for each BUGS model:

1) direct translation of the BUGS models, preserving priors

2) model with our preferred priors

So while they're mostly there, they're in various stages
of having both versions for each model and (2) being up to our
current coding practices (vectorization, priors, etc.)

For example, the very first example in the vol1 needs to be
updated:

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker

I'm assuming this is a reasonable direct translation (though maybe using the regular
binomial instead of binomial-logit would be more faithful, we're more concerned
about having the same model than the same coding, so algebraic differences like
binomial(inv_logit(alpha)) vs. binomial_logit(alpha) shouldn't matter).

What we want is a "best practices" version with weakly informative priors as
recommended in the regression chapter of the manual.

We'd also love to get simulations going for all these models, but that's
a secondary concern.

For the ARM models, they all need to be tested --- I think many of them
are broken.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Translation of examples in Hill, Gelman books into Stan code
parts:
I’d actually argue that simulations are paramount!

Recall that we have two problems: is our fit parsimonious with the
given model and is our model parsimonious with the “truth”?
Simulated data and our diagnostics checks the former, PPCs
check the latter.

I think it’d be great if for every example we had:

Step 1:
Simulate data from the model
Fit the model to the simulated data
Check diagnostics (n_divergent is zero for all iterations, tree_depth < max_depth for all iterations, R_hat < 1.1)
— if diagnostics fail improve model with a note explaining the fix
Check fit to exact results
— if fit is poor then improve model with a note explaining the fix

Step 2:
Fit the model to the true data
Check diagnostics (n_divergent is zero for all iterations, tree_depth < max_depth for all iterations, R_hat < 1.1)
— if diagnostics fail improve model with a note explaining the fix
Check posterior predictive checks
— if PPCs are bad improve model with a note explaining the fix

Basically, we want to encourage people to always see if they can recover the results from
simulated data before moving on to evaluating their model with PPCs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Translation of examples in Hill, Gelman books into Stan code
parts:
Firstly, divergences during warmup are ignorable as they usually typically
denote poor steps in the adaptation instead of pathologies in the sampler.
So if the divergences are really occurring only in the first 1000 iterations
then you’re fine.

It’s only when you see divergences in the sampling phase that you have
to worry.  In this case manually specifying a step size will not be sufficient
because the adaptation will rapidly change the initial value (although
setting a lower step size can sometimes speed up adaptation if larger
step sizes lead to awkward parameter values and expensive likelihood
computations).  What you have to do is increase the target acceptance
probability (change “delta” parameter from the default 0.8 to 0.9 or
higher as necessary for removing the divergences).

For more see http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.

parts:
Thanks --- that looks awesome. Much more than we were
expecting. Although it'd be great, the key thing is getting
the code for both the BUGS model and "best practices" model right.

Your updated model looks great!

As to the direct translation, it's fine as is, but it doesn't have
to be literally line for line. I think it's OK to translate the model,
not the implementation. So it's OK to use, for example, binomial_logit
in the translation. This is really a judgment call, but I'd rather
err on the side of efficient Stan idioms as long as we literally
translate the model as written to one with the same posterior.
Maybe some bread crumbs in the text on the translation?

Then we want to provide the model we would've used.

Some specific comments:

* Num -> N

* keep the opening curly brace on the same line as the for statement
(we basically follow the Google code style in Stan as well as in
C++).

* spaces after commas (e.g., in gamma(0.001, 0.001))

* space between operators ("1 / sqrt(tau)" rather than "1.0/sqrt(tau)").

* Indentation in code needs to be right. No tabs and everything
indented 2 spaces. You missed the indent on the binomial lines
and all of the generated quantities block. There's an emacs mode
that'll clean this up for you automatically if you get everything
on the right lines. We're not entirely consistent yet in the manual
and elsewhere, but we're aiming for it.

* I think instead of "1 / 1E-6" as your scale, you just want "1e3",
that is, sd = 1 / sqrt(tau).

* I'd just define sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau) as a transformed parameter
and then use it in the student_t (sampling statement in model and
rng in generated quantities), and eliminate sigma from generated quantities

* The fake data script is for the original model; I'm not sure if
we want it for both models or just our form?

* It'd be nice if we could do the simulation in Stan, too --- the R
interface isn't really set up to do it very easily, but it's possible
to run for a single iteration with generated quantities and no params and
then pull out structured values --- just some awkward index fiddling.
But then there's also something to be said for standalone fake data
generation.

* always a space after commas, even in R

* Table 3 should be a plot with actual value on the x axis and fitted
value with some interval on the y axis (geom_errorbars or something like
that in ggplot2); it could be faceted by top-level param name

* diagnostic discussion is great, but it should probably be 4.1, not 4.0.3.

* n_{\mathrm{eff}} and n_{\mathrm{leapfrog}} and \hat{R} in LaTeX

* I didn't understand the point of table 4 --- they're comparing different
models and most of the BUGS entries are missing anyway

* The code after table 4 needs indentation

* Instead of


if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i])
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
}
else
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
}

indent as

if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]) {
indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
} else {
indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
}

but what you really want to do is this:

indicatorTreat[i] <- (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]);

* $p$-values, I think --- isn't the p usually italicized? I don't
know for sure as I don't do much with them.

* If you cite BDA, it should be BDA3

* Your bib form is messing up capitalization of journals for some reason

* Also, you need our fonts to get the code blocks right --- LaTeX messes
up ~ as a matter of course in most fonts, conflating it with the diacritic

Your updated model looks great!

As to the direct translation, it's fine as is, but it doesn't have
to be literally line for line.  I think it's OK to translate the model,
not the implementation.  So it's OK to use, for example, binomial_logit
in the translation.  This is really a judgment call, but I'd rather
err on the side of efficient Stan idioms as long as we literally
translate the model as written to one with the same posterior.
Maybe some bread crumbs in the text on the translation?

Then we want to provide the model we would've used.

Some specific comments:

* Num -> N

* keep the opening curly brace on the same line as the for statement
  (we basically follow the Google code style in Stan as well as in
   C++).
* spaces after commas (e.g., in gamma(0.001, 0.001))

* space between operators ("1 / sqrt(tau)" rather than "1.0/sqrt(tau)").

* Indentation in code needs to be right.  No tabs and everything
  indented 2 spaces.  You missed the indent on the binomial lines
  and all of the generated quantities block.  There's an emacs mode
  that'll clean this up for you automatically if you get everything
  on the right lines.  We're not entirely consistent yet in the manual
  and elsewhere, but we're aiming for it.

* I think instead of "1 / 1E-6" as your scale, you just want "1e3",
  that is, sd = 1 / sqrt(tau).

* I'd just define sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau) as a transformed parameter
  and then use it in the student_t (sampling statement in model and
  rng in generated quantities), and eliminate sigma from generated quantities

* The fake data script is for the original model;  I'm not sure if
  we want it for both models or just our form?

* It'd be nice if we could do the simulation in Stan, too --- the R
  interface isn't really set up to do it very easily, but it's possible
  to run for a single iteration with generated quantities and no params and
  then pull out structured values --- just some awkward index fiddling.
  But then there's also something to be said for standalone fake data
  generation.

* always a space after commas, even in R

* Table 3 should be a plot with actual value on the x axis and fitted
  value with some interval on the y axis (geom_errorbars or something like
  that in ggplot2);  it could be faceted by top-level param name

* diagnostic discussion is great, but it should probably be 4.1, not 4.0.3.

* n_{\mathrm{eff}} and n_{\mathrm{leapfrog}} and \hat{R} in LaTeX

* I didn't understand the point of table 4 --- they're comparing different
  models and most of the BUGS entries are missing anyway

* The code after table 4 needs indentation

* Instead of


if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i])
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
}
else
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
}

indent as

 if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]) {
   indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
 } else {
   indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
 }

but what you really want to do is this:

  indicatorTreat[i] <- (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]);

* $p$-values, I think --- isn't the p usually italicized?  I don't
  know for sure as I don't do much with them.

* If you cite BDA, it should be BDA3

* Your bib form is messing up capitalization of journals for some reason

* Also, you need our fonts to get the code blocks right --- LaTeX messes
  up ~ as a matter of course in most fonts, conflating it with the diacritic
  tilde.

- Bob

Thanks --- that looks fantastic. Are you generating the LaTeX
through knitr?

I like the plot with all the parameter values, but this style's going
to get problematic when the parameters aren't all on the same scale.
If I were doing it, I'd facet the different named parameters through
ggplot2. But this is already way more than we need in this context,
so I'm not suggesting redoing it!

In general, I think 90% intervals are OK --- the problem is that
the larger the interval, the noisier the endpoint estimates are.

It's great that you plotted that we get the same result as BUGS.
Could you indicate if it's OpenBUGS or WinBUGS and which version?

The overlplotting of orange and blue (great color choice, by the
way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think
it's a big deal. What is an issue is that you probably want to be
comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
converge to the same value if everything's working.

And to compare apples and apples, you need to do both with Stan's
method of computing n_eff. I have some code to convert R2jags
output to something Stan can process.

The bibliography's still messed up in terms of capitalization.
(And "2x 2" rather than "2 x 2".)

You want to use "a---b" for em-dashes to separate text in
American English typesetting (you get an extra space in the UK,
but you also want to use the em-dash).

The values 1 and 0 shouldn't be quoted. A quote usually
indicates a character rather than the value.

Spaces, so it's not [0.025,0.975], but [0.025, 0.975].

And remember, 95% intervals are going to be noisier than,
say 80% intervals. In both cases, you can calibrate by eye.

Sorry for all the typesetting comments --- I'm a nut about it,
but it's all minor stuff compared to the content.

- Bob

P.S. Some R to fit a JAGS model (for an IRT example) and then
pull out the effective sample sizes. It's not complete, as
there are dependencies on things like num_params, but I hope it's
clear what's going on (the relevant bit is the monitor and n_eff
extraction, which Ben showed me how to do):

start_time_jags <- proc.time();

fit_jags <- jags(model.file = "irt.jags",
data = list(I=I, J=J, y=y),
init = init_list,
parameters.to.save = c("alpha","beta","delta"),
n.chains = num_chains,
n.iter = 10000,
jags.seed = init_seed);

elapsed_time_jags = proc.time() - start_time_jags;
print(c("jags", elapsed_time_jags));

fit_jags_mcmc <- as.mcmc(fit_jags);
arr <- as.array(fit_jags_mcmc);
arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2));
mon <- monitor(arr, inc_warmup = FALSE);

n_eff_jags <- mon[1:num_params, "n_eff"];
sec_jags <- elapsed_time_jags[3];
n_eff_per_sec_jags <- n_eff_jags / sec_jags;

Yes, I will include this information, FYI it's OpenBUGS. version 3.2.3. rev 1012.

way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think

it's a big deal.  What is an issue is that you probably want to be
comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
converge to the same value if everything's working.
Ok. I will redo with the plot with these.

And to compare apples and apples, you need to do both with Stan's
method of computing n_eff.  I have some code to convert R2jags
output to something Stan can process.

Ok, is there a style that you recommend? At the moment I am just using 'plain'.

You want to use "a---b" for em-dashes to separate text in
American English typesetting (you get an extra space in the UK,
but you also want to use the em-dash).

indicates a character rather than the value.
Ok.
Spaces, so it's not [0.025,0.975], but [0.025, 0.975].
Yep, my mistake. Will change.

say 80% intervals.  In both cases, you can calibrate by eye.

Sorry for all the typesetting comments --- I'm a nut about it,
but it's all minor stuff compared to the content.

- Bob

P.S.  Some R to fit a JAGS model (for an IRT example) and then
pull out the effective sample sizes.  It's not complete, as
there are dependencies on things like num_params, but I hope it's
clear what's going on (the relevant bit is the monitor and n_eff
extraction, which Ben showed me how to do):

start_time_jags <- proc.time();

fit_jags <- jags(model.file = "irt.jags",
                 data = list(I=I, J=J, y=y),
                 init = init_list,
                 parameters.to.save = c("alpha","beta","delta"),
                 n.chains = num_chains,
                 n.iter = 10000,
                 jags.seed = init_seed);

elapsed_time_jags = proc.time() - start_time_jags;
print(c("jags", elapsed_time_jags));

fit_jags_mcmc <- as.mcmc(fit_jags);
arr <- as.array(fit_jags_mcmc);
arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2));
mon <- monitor(arr, inc_warmup = FALSE);

n_eff_jags <- mon[1:num_params, "n_eff"];
sec_jags <- elapsed_time_jags[3];
n_eff_per_sec_jags <- n_eff_jags / sec_jags;

df_stan <- data.frame(n_eff_per_sec = n_eff_per_sec_stan,

Regarding the diagnostics:

The n_leapfrog isn’t technically what you want to be looking for, and is
mostly redundant with treedepth anyways, so I’d just look at divergences
and treedepth. I actually like showing a histogram of treedepth here, with
a line at 10, but this count is fine.

Also you have to be really careful with the language — the diagnostics
passing do not indicate convergence/mixing but rather show no signs of
non-convergence/non-mixing. This is a subtle but important point as
we can never guarantee convergence.

Additionally you don’t quote how many chains you run. I’d make this
explicit in the call and emphasize the robustness given by running
multiple chains.

> The overlplotting of orange and blue (great color choice, by the
> way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think
> it's a big deal. What is an issue is that you probably want to be
> comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
> converge to the same value if everything's working.

As Bob noted we really want to be treating Stan as the baseline and
(hoping) that we’re geometrically ergodic so the MCMC std error means
something. Assuming that this is true then what I’d recommend is

(a) rescale each parameter by subtracting the Stan mean and then
dividing by the Stan MCMC std error.

(b) The Stan parameters are all now N(0, 1) and can be represented
by a solid band from -2 to 2.

(c) Now you can plot the BUGS results as points + bars representing
the standardized means +/- 2 standardized deviations. Everything will
be on a consistent scale and deviations will be easy to spot.

You can do a similar resealing with the simulated data, only given that
the simulated data is exact you won’t need a band (just a line at 0) and
you’d want to use posterior quantiles (as you already do in Figure 1).
It would be great to see this particular plot for both Stan and BUGS.

Additionally Bob noted that performance is important. I recommend
adding a quick “Performance” section and plotting histograms of
n_eff / time for all parameters, one histogram for BUGS and one for
Stan. This can be done by overlapping transparent histograms on
one plot or just having two separate figures.
